network.overall_strategy: This is an evidence-qualified candidate network, not ten experimentally established syntheses. Ten distinct reaction sequences are enumerated: direct electrical-discharge formation; proposed indole–pyruvate coupling; and paired hydroxymethyl/Mannich entry routes into Strecker, aminomalononitrile, and indole-acetate chemistry. The indole-acetate branch has separate reductive-amination and transamination exits. These sequences share chemically necessary modules and are not ten independent mechanisms. The expanded graph contains 26 molecules and 24 reactions to expose, rather than conceal, intermediate and activation requirements. Only the discharge endpoint has direct laboratory evidence for tryptophan formation from simple feed gases; its mechanism and absolute yield remain unresolved. Every indole-based pathway includes an explicitly unresolved indole-assembly node. Additional unsupported transformations are marked speculative, and their conditions are candidate testing windows rather than established protocols. All settings are anoxic. Hot carbonylation, cooler reducing chemistry, and surface concentration occur in separate reaction zones, not one vessel; their integration and transport efficiencies remain unproven. Indole-containing products require opaque mineral, sediment, or subsurface shielding from surface UV. No enzymes, molecular oxygen, or biological cofactors are assumed. Structures use neutral reference forms despite aqueous acid–base speciation. Tryptophan has unspecified stereochemistry, with racemic production expected absent an independently demonstrated selection mechanism. Its environment_formed is null because several environments produce the same target node. The tentative Bennu detection is evidence of possible occurrence, not a separate synthesis mechanism (Mojarro et al., 2025).

reactions.name: Observed electrical-discharge tryptophan formation, unresolved product channel

conditions.temperature: 353 K water reservoir; discharge is a nonequilibrium energy source
conditions.pressure: Gas-circulation apparatus; exact operating pressure not specified in the supplied report
conditions.other: Anoxic CH4/NH3/H2 atmosphere, electrical discharge for 3–7 days, and replenished methane and ammonia. Tungsten electrodes supply the discharge and are not assigned selective catalytic activity. Hydrogen appears on both sides because it is supplied in the atmosphere and may also be evolved in the formal selected-product balance.

reactions.mechanism: Coarse-grained experimental endpoint encompassing gas activation, aqueous product accumulation, and unresolved heteroaromatic and amino-acid chemistry. No tryptophan-specific sequence is assigned.
reactions.reasoning: Jiang et al. (2014) detected tryptophan in discharge products from these simple gases. This supports formation, not a resolved mechanism or quantified absolute tryptophan yield; the reported 4.3 mg belongs to a separate experiment using commercial tryptophan. This node represents a selected product channel, not the complete discharge mixture. Transient, replenished reducing atmospheres are more defensible than a permanently NH3-rich global atmosphere (Kasting, 1982; Hashimoto et al., 2007).

reactions.name: Discharge production of hydrogen cyanide and formaldehyde

conditions.temperature: 300–353 K collecting water; nonequilibrium discharge zone
conditions.pressure: Approximately ambient in the proposed environmental analogue
conditions.other: Locally reducing, continuously replenished gases; rapid dissolution of soluble products into sheltered water. Product volatilization and photolysis compete with collection.

reactions.mechanism: Electrical fragmentation and radical recombination generate nitrile and carbonyl pools that dissolve in water. The node lumps multiple reactions rather than asserting a selective elementary conversion.
reactions.reasoning: HCN and carbonyl accumulation underpin the general discharge–Strecker interpretation established by Miller (1957). Jiang et al. (2014) support the relevance of a reducing discharge setting, but neither study establishes the specific downstream indole chemistry represented here. Ammonia replenishment and collection efficiency are environmental constraints.

reactions.name: Unresolved hydrothermal indole assembly: thermodynamic gap node

conditions.temperature: 373 K thermodynamic reference; not a demonstrated synthesis temperature
conditions.pressure: Subseafloor pressure maintaining an aqueous phase
conditions.other: H2-rich fluid near pH 8.5. CO2 represents the inorganic-carbon pool, largely bicarbonate under these conditions. No validated catalyst, residence time, or selective ring-assembly sequence is available.

reactions.mechanism: Unresolved multistep reduction, carbon–carbon coupling, nitrogen incorporation, and fused-ring formation. This is a formal net conversion, not an elementary or kinetically established reaction.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative and presently unclosed. Ménez et al. (2018) calculated favorable bulk indole-formation thermodynamics for a modeled H2-rich fluid, but did not demonstrate conversion of inorganic carbon to indole. No mineral is assigned merely because it occurs in serpentinite. This explicit gap prevents commercially available indole from being silently treated as a simple geochemical feedstock.

reactions.name: FeS-associated CO/thiol carbonylation to pyruvate
agents: Iron(II) sulfide: reactive mineral agent in carbonyl chemistry

conditions.catalyst: FeS-associated carbonyl species; catalytic regeneration is not assumed
conditions.other: CO- and thiol-bearing reducing fluid. This hot precursor-production zone is separate from every indole- and tryptophan-containing zone. Cooling and export are required before downstream use.

reactions.mechanism: Lumped mineral-associated carbonylation of a methyl-sulfur feedstock, represented by an atom-balanced selected-product channel to pyruvic acid and hydrogen sulfide.
reactions.reasoning: Cody et al. (2000) experimentally support pyruvate formation within high-pressure CO/alkyl-thiol/FeS chemistry. The simplified channel does not claim that a clean elementary double carbonylation or selective yield was demonstrated. Hot-zone segregation is necessary because tryptophan decomposes readily in hot compressed water (Sheehan and Savage, 2020).

reactions.name: Proposed Fe-saponite-mediated indole–pyruvate–ammonia coupling
agents: Fe-rich saponite: proposed adsorption and acid-catalysis surface

conditions.temperature: 350–383 K; 373 K is the published thermodynamic reference
conditions.catalyst: Fe-rich saponite, proposed rather than experimentally validated for this conversion
conditions.other: Cool H2-rich alteration zone near pH 8–9 with locally acidic mineral sites. Surface acidity does not imply molecular oxygen or oxidation of the organic substrate. Product retention and shielding are required.

reactions.mechanism: Hypothesized pyruvate/ammonia activation followed by indole C3 attachment to the terminal side-chain carbon. An aminoacrylate-like or equivalent activated intermediate would be needed; its mineral-mediated generation is unresolved.
reactions.reasoning: Ménez et al. (2018) proposed a Friedel–Crafts-type route from the natural Fe-saponite association, not a reproduced synthesis. Simple indole attack on the pyruvate ketone would give the wrong connectivity, so the required side-chain activation is an explicit bottleneck. Enzyme-assisted reversibility establishes overall chemical feasibility but not abiotic kinetics (Watanabe and Snell, 1972; Tewari and Goldberg, 1994).

reactions.name: C3 hydroxymethylation of indole

conditions.catalyst: General-acid catalysis; no specific mineral is required
conditions.other: Concentrated, UV-shielded water films with controlled formaldehyde exposure and mild acidity. Excessive acid exposure favors oligomerization and bis-indolyl products.

reactions.mechanism: Indole undergoes electrophilic substitution at C3 by activated formaldehyde, followed by rearomatization to the hydroxymethyl derivative.
reactions.reasoning: Kuroda and Kobayashi (2024) use indole hydroxymethylation as a chemically plausible side-chain precursor module. This is ordinary indole reactivity, but selective accumulation in a geochemical mixture and linkage to tryptophan synthesis remain unvalidated. Formaldehyde availability alone does not solve indole production or product preservation.

reactions.name: Hypothesized ammonia-based Mannich entry to 3-aminomethylindole

conditions.other: Sheltered concentrated films near neutral pH with ammonia/formaldehyde turnover. Monoaminomethylation must compete with aminal formation, multiple substitution, and formaldehyde–ammonia sequestration.

reactions.mechanism: An ammonia/formaldehyde-derived imine or iminium equivalent is trapped at indole C3, giving a primary aminomethyl substituent after proton transfer.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative extension not demonstrated in the supplied prebiotic studies. Its chemical merit is that an aminomethyl group could provide a different leaving-group precursor for side-chain transfer, rather than requiring displacement of an unactivated alcohol. Conventional indole Mannich reactivity does not establish selective formation of this ammonia-derived primary amine; it must not be confused with experimentally established gramine synthesis using dimethylamine.

reactions.name: Hypothesized cyanide trapping of activated indole-3-carbinol
agents: Aqueous proton donors: proposed leaving-group activation

conditions.catalyst: General-acid activation in a staged acid–base microenvironment
conditions.other: Alcohol activation and cyanide capture require compatible adjacent or sequential microenvironments. HCN/CN speciation, volatilization, and indole oligomerization are major constraints; no successful prebiotic pH program is established.

reactions.mechanism: Loss of water from the activated hydroxymethyl derivative generates an indolylmethyl electrophile that is trapped through the carbon atom of cyanide.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative as a linked prebiotic transformation. It implements the indole–formaldehyde–cyanide proposal summarized in the supplied report, with hydroxymethylation motivated by Kuroda and Kobayashi (2024). The report supplies no selective geochemical demonstration of this cyanation, and acidic activation conflicts with maintaining appreciable free cyanide.

reactions.name: Hypothesized cyanide substitution of an aminomethylindole precursor

conditions.other: Partially protonated aminomethyl precursor in HCN/CN-containing sheltered films. A productive overlap between leaving-group activation and cyanide availability is unestablished.

reactions.mechanism: Protonation facilitates ammonia departure from the aminomethyl substituent; cyanide captures the resulting indolylmethyl electrophile. Proton transfers are included in the net reaction.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative; no supplied study demonstrates this transformation under prebiotic conditions. It is retained as a chemically distinct alternative to alcohol displacement because ammonia can be a leaving group after protonation. Productive substitution must outcompete indole condensation, precursor decomposition, and reversal of the Mannich reaction.

reactions.name: Unvalidated selective nitrile reduction and hydrolysis to tryptaldehyde
agents: Native Ni-bearing Fe–Ni alloy: candidate hydrogen-activation surface

conditions.pressure: Elevated H2-bearing aqueous pressure; 5–20 MPa is a scenario assumption
conditions.catalyst: Native Ni-bearing Fe–Ni alloy, unvalidated for selective aldehyde production
conditions.other: Requires rapid hydrolysis or desorption of a partially reduced nitrile before further hydrogenation. Metal availability, sulfide poisoning, and transport from the surface-generated nitrile pool remain unresolved.

reactions.mechanism: Partial hydrogenation of the nitrile gives an imine that hydrolyzes to indole-3-acetaldehyde and ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative and a major bottleneck: no supplied study establishes this selective prebiotic conversion. A metal surface can motivate hydrogen activation, but it may instead hydrogenate the nitrile completely to tryptamine or reduce other groups. This explicit gap supplies the aldehyde required by Strecker chemistry without pretending that the general mechanism in Miller (1957) explains the aldehyde's origin.

reactions.name: Tryptaldehyde–ammonia imine formation

conditions.other: Concentrated, sheltered films with sufficient free ammonia; partial water loss may favor condensation. The imine is an equilibrium intermediate and need not accumulate as an isolated compound.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia adds to the aldehyde, producing a carbinolamine that loses water to form the imine.
reactions.reasoning: This is the established carbonyl–ammonia component of Strecker chemistry (Miller, 1957). Applying it to tryptaldehyde is chemically conventional, but the supplied research does not demonstrate an integrated tryptophan-specific prebiotic sequence. Aldehyde instability and the unresolved preceding reduction remain limiting.

reactions.name: Cyanide addition to the tryptaldehyde imine

conditions.other: HCN/CN-containing ammonia-buffered solution with a compatible imine/iminium population. Competing cyanohydrin formation and HCN polymerization are not assumed absent.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide adds to the imine carbon and proton transfer gives the alpha-aminonitrile, creating the future amino-acid stereocenter without imposed stereoselection.
reactions.reasoning: The elementary Strecker reaction is well established (Miller, 1957). Its extension to an indole-substituted imine is chemically plausible but is not a demonstrated source of Jiang et al.'s (2014) tryptophan. Neither an enantiomeric excess nor a useful product selectivity is inferred.

reactions.name: Tryptophan aminonitrile hydrolysis

conditions.catalyst: Alkaline solution; hydroxide promotes hydrolysis and acid–base speciation
conditions.other: Candidate pH 10–11, prolonged residence, and opaque shielding. Neutral acid and ammonia formulas represent the corresponding aqueous ionic pools. Neither rate nor recovery of tryptophan is established at this window.

reactions.mechanism: Sequential nitrile hydration and amide hydrolysis convert the nitrile carbon into the carboxyl group and release ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Aminonitrile hydrolysis is the canonical terminal Strecker step (Miller, 1957), but the supplied research gives no validated mild-condition hydrolysis yield for this particular substrate. Conditions must avoid trading slow hydrolysis for indole degradation; product shielding is necessary because aqueous tryptophan photodegrades (Scappini et al., 2007).

reactions.name: HCN oligomerization into an aminomalononitrile pool

conditions.other: Concentrated, weakly alkaline HCN/CN chemistry in sheltered films. This node selects the formal trimer channel from a complex oligomer mixture and does not imply selective aminomalononitrile accumulation.

reactions.mechanism: HCN oligomerization and proton-transfer chemistry generate a formal three-HCN amino-dinitrile scaffold.
reactions.reasoning: Kuroda and Kobayashi (2024) discuss aminomalononitrile as an HCN-derived glycine-equivalent precursor. Its participation in a tryptophan synthesis is hypothetical. Continued oligomerization, hydrolysis, and the limited lifetime of a reactive aminomalononitrile pool are important competing processes.

reactions.name: Proposed C-alkylation of aminomalononitrile by indole-3-carbinol
agents: General-acid/base proton donors and acceptors: hypothetical activation system

conditions.other: Concentrated sheltered films with staged electrophile generation and nucleophile availability. No established pH window simultaneously ensures productive alcohol activation, aminomalononitrile C-reactivity, and substrate stability.

reactions.mechanism: A carbon-centered aminomalononitrile nucleophile captures an activated indolylmethyl electrophile, replacing the scaffold's central hydrogen with the indolylmethyl side chain.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative implementation of the glycine-equivalent/side-chain topology discussed by Kuroda and Kobayashi (2024), not a reported tryptophan experiment. Carbon alkylation must outcompete nitrogen alkylation, HCN oligomer chemistry, and indole condensation. The competing activation requirements are an explicit bottleneck.

reactions.name: Proposed aminomalononitrile C-alkylation through ammonia displacement
agents: General-acid/base proton donors and acceptors: hypothetical activation system

conditions.other: Requires protonation-assisted amino-group departure while preserving a carbon-nucleophilic glycine-equivalent pool. No successful prebiotic concentration or pH regime is established.

reactions.mechanism: The carbon center of aminomalononitrile captures the indolylmethyl electrophile generated by ammonia departure from the aminomethyl precursor.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative extension with no direct support in the supplied experiments. It applies the scaffold-alkylation concept of Kuroda and Kobayashi (2024) to a different leaving-group precursor. Its chemical distinction from the alcohol route is genuine, but its feasibility and selectivity must be tested rather than inferred from the pathway count.

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of the substituted amino-dinitrile

conditions.other: Candidate pH 10–11 with extended residence and UV exclusion. Both nitrile groups must hydrolyze; partially hydrolyzed intermediates and decomposition are expected competitors.

reactions.mechanism: Both nitriles undergo hydration and amide hydrolysis, yielding a substituted aminomalonic acid and ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative for this substrate under these conditions. It is the chemically explicit hydrolysis required to turn the aminomalononitrile framework discussed by Kuroda and Kobayashi (2024) into an amino-acid precursor. General nitrile hydrolysis does not establish preservation of this sterically congested, indole-containing substrate.

reactions.name: Substituted aminomalonic-acid decarboxylation

conditions.other: A partially protonated carboxyl population after the hydrolysis stage; sheltered warm films with product removal. A useful decarboxylation rate at this temperature has not been established.

reactions.mechanism: Loss of one carboxyl group as CO2, followed by proton transfer, converts the substituted aminomalonic skeleton into tryptophan.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative in the prebiotic tryptophan setting, although malonic-acid decarboxylation provides a conventional structural rationale. This is the necessary carbon-loss step for the explicit aminomalononitrile implementation of Kuroda and Kobayashi's (2024) proposal. It does not supply evidence for the preceding selective alkylation or a complete sequence.

reactions.name: Indole-3-acetonitrile hydrolysis to indole acetate

conditions.other: Candidate pH 10–11, long residence, and opaque shielding. The represented neutral acid will be predominantly indole acetate at alkaline pH.

reactions.mechanism: Nitrile hydration followed by amide hydrolysis generates the carboxyl group of indole-3-acetic acid and releases ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Chemically conventional but speculative as an integrated prebiotic step at the proposed window. The supplied report includes nitrile hydrolysis in its historical indole-acetate framework, without a complete experimental sequence or substrate-specific rate. This branch avoids selective partial nitrile reduction but introduces the harder subsequent acyl activation and carboxylation requirements.

reactions.name: Unresolved activation of indole acetate as a methyl thioester

conditions.other: Concentrated drying film supplied with methanethiol. No validated activating reagent or catalyst is supplied by the research; volatile thiol loss, unfavorable condensation, and rehydration are unresolved.

reactions.mechanism: Formal condensation of the carboxylic acid with methanethiol to create an acyl thioester. The actual activation mechanism remains missing.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative activation-gap node, not a claim that wet–dry cycling alone efficiently makes this thioester. It is included because reductive carboxylation of a free carboxylate cannot be assumed to proceed like enzyme-mediated acyl chemistry. Cody et al. (2000) support sulfur-associated carbonyl chemistry generally, not this indoleacetate esterification. An activated acyl carrier or alternative verified mechanism is still required.

reactions.name: Hypothesized reductive carboxylation of activated indole acetate
agents: Fe/Ni sulfide interface: candidate acyl-binding and hydrogen-activation surface

conditions.pressure: Elevated H2-bearing aqueous pressure; 5–20 MPa is a scenario assumption
conditions.catalyst: Fe/Ni sulfides, hypothetical for this carboxylation
conditions.other: Strongly reducing pore fluid near pH 7–9. H2 denotes a formal electron source; sufficiently low-potential electron delivery to the acyl intermediate is not established. Thioester hydrolysis competes with reaction.

reactions.mechanism: Formal reductive acyl activation and CO2 incorporation convert the thioester into an alpha-keto acid, releasing methanethiol. A selective nonenzymatic electron-transfer sequence is unresolved.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative and a major energetic and kinetic bottleneck. The microbial indole-acetate work from 1974 summarized in the supplied report establishes only biological feasibility, not an H2/mineral pathway. Novikov and Copley (2013) support mineral-dependent keto-acid transformations, not this reductive carboxylation. Mineral binding and H2 activation alone do not demonstrate that the required acyl intermediate can form.

reactions.name: Proposed reductive amination of indolepyruvate

conditions.catalyst: Fe/Ni sulfides, extrapolated from simpler keto-acid chemistry
conditions.other: Ammonia-containing reducing fluid near pH 7–9; opaque pore confinement and prompt cooling or retention. Carbonyl reduction to indolelactate and decarboxylation may compete.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia condenses with the alpha-keto group; reduction of the resulting imine gives the alpha-amino-acid functionality.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative for indolepyruvate under this mineral/H2 regime. Novikov and Copley (2013) provide support for mineral-dependent reactions and reductive amination of simpler keto acids, not a demonstrated tryptophan yield. Substrate-dependent selectivity, hydrogen activation, and tryptophan preservation require independent testing.

reactions.name: Mineral-associated pyruvate reductive amination to alanine

conditions.temperature: 350–383 K, within the broader mild hydrothermal range surveyed
conditions.catalyst: Transition-metal sulfides; activity depends on mineral identity and redox state
conditions.other: Ammonia-bearing fluid near pH 7–9. H2 represents the network's reducing-equivalent source; its effective coupling to the chosen mineral assemblage must be verified.

reactions.mechanism: Pyruvate forms an ammonia-derived imine, followed by reduction to alanine.
reactions.reasoning: Small-keto-acid reductive amination has independent experimental support in mineral systems (Novikov and Copley, 2013). The selected assemblage and formal H2 coupling are scenario assumptions rather than an exact reproduction of every reported experiment. Alanine is included specifically as the amino donor for the alternative transamination exit, not merely as an unrelated amino-acid product.

reactions.name: Hypothesized nonenzymatic alanine-to-indolepyruvate transamination

conditions.catalyst: Fe(II) coordination, unvalidated for this substrate pair
conditions.other: Concentrated, UV-shielded mineral-interface water near pH 7–9. No pyridoxal phosphate, protein, or enzyme is assumed. Pyruvate is regenerated as the amino-donor coproduct.

reactions.mechanism: A Schiff-base exchange between alanine and indolepyruvate, coupled to proton transfer and hydrolysis, formally transfers the amino group to the aromatic keto acid.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative; no supplied study demonstrates this enzyme-free substrate pair. The report's indole-acetate framework invokes transamination, but biological feasibility cannot be transferred directly to a mineral interface. Fe(II) is proposed for carbonyl/imine coordination, not because abundant iron guarantees catalysis. Slow proton transfer, imine hydrolysis, and competing decarboxylation may prevent useful conversion.

pathways.name: Direct reducing-atmosphere discharge
pathways.description: The only listed route with direct laboratory detection of tryptophan from simple feed gases. The single reaction node is an unresolved experimental product channel, not a one-step mechanism or a quantified synthesis.

pathways.name: Hydrothermal indole–pyruvate coupling
pathways.description: Indole from an unresolved inorganic-carbon assembly module and pyruvate from a separate hot carbonylation module meet in cooler Fe-saponite-bearing pores. Natural association and thermodynamics support investigation, but neither indole assembly nor selective tryptophan coupling is experimentally closed.

pathways.name: Hydroxymethyl entry to aldehyde–Strecker synthesis
pathways.description: Discharge-derived formaldehyde and HCN functionalize indole through its hydroxymethyl derivative. Selective nitrile reduction supplies tryptaldehyde for ordinary Strecker chemistry. Indole assembly, cyanation, and especially aldehyde-selective reduction remain unvalidated; reducing-pore and surface-condensation stages require compatible transport.

pathways.name: Mannich entry to aldehyde–Strecker synthesis
pathways.description: An ammonia-derived aminomethylindole replaces the alcohol precursor as the proposed cyanide-substitution substrate. The route then shares nitrile reduction and Strecker chemistry with P3. Its distinct Mannich entry adds an explicitly speculative selectivity requirement rather than constituting an independently established synthesis.

pathways.name: Hydroxymethyl alkylation of an HCN-derived amino-acid scaffold
pathways.description: Indole hydroxymethylation and HCN oligomerization provide separate side-chain and aminomalononitrile modules. Proposed carbon-selective alkylation, double nitrile hydrolysis, and decarboxylation produce the target skeleton. This is an explicit hypothesis derived from the glycine-equivalent framework, not a demonstrated CGP or tryptophan experiment.

pathways.name: Mannich side-chain transfer to an HCN-derived amino-acid scaffold
pathways.description: The proposed aminomethylindole precursor transfers its indolylmethyl group to aminomalononitrile with ammonia departure. Hydrolysis and decarboxylation are shared with P5. Primary-amine formation, carbon-selective substitution, and compatible activation conditions are unresolved.

pathways.name: Hydroxymethyl–indoleacetate route with reductive amination
pathways.description: The hydroxymethyl/cyanide route supplies indoleacetonitrile, which is hydrolyzed rather than partially reduced. Explicit but unresolved thioester activation and reductive carboxylation furnish indolepyruvate, followed by candidate reductive amination. Activation, low-potential electron delivery, and thioester survival during transfer are major gaps.

pathways.name: Mannich–indoleacetate route with reductive amination
pathways.description: Aminomethylindole is the proposed entry to indoleacetonitrile. The downstream acid, activated-acyl, reductive-carboxylation, and reductive-amination sequence is shared with P7. This is a distinct graph sequence, not independent experimental evidence for the shared transformations.

pathways.name: Hydroxymethyl–indoleacetate route with alanine transamination
pathways.description: The hydroxymethyl/indoleacetate sequence supplies indolepyruvate. A separate pyruvate reductive-amination module supplies alanine, whose amino group is then formally transferred to indolepyruvate, regenerating pyruvate. This exit differs chemically from direct reductive amination, but enzyme-free transamination of this pair remains unvalidated.

pathways.name: Mannich–indoleacetate route with alanine transamination
pathways.description: The aminomethyl entry supplies the indoleacetate branch, while independently formed pyruvate supplies alanine. Proposed Fe(II)-assisted amino-group transfer closes the target sequence. This combines distinct entry and exit chemistry while retaining all indole-production, activation, carboxylation, and transamination gaps.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Jiang et al. (2014) directly supports detectable tryptophan formation from the listed reducing gases and water. Representing rxn_001 as an empirical, unresolved product channel is appropriate; it is not an established elementary reaction. Unknown mechanism and absolute yield limit quantitative network modeling but do not negate the reported endpoint. The surface setting is plausible for a locally replenished reducing gas system, although gas composition, discharge exposure, product capture and preservation are not quantitatively specified.
suggestions: Retain the empirical-channel designation and attach Jiang et al. (2014) directly to rxn_001, without assigning an unproven Strecker mechanism.
Specify gas replenishment, discharge exposure, water temperature and shielded product collection; measure absolute tryptophan yield, blanks and isotope incorporation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The precursor arrangement is formally coherent, and Cody et al. (2000) provides experimental support for the pyruvate module. However, rxn_003 is a thermodynamic net transformation rather than a demonstrated indole synthesis. For rxn_005, the Fe-saponite association and thermodynamic arguments of Ménez et al. (2018) do not establish mineral-catalyzed formation of the required indol-3-yl–CH2–CH(NH2)–CO2H connectivity. Separating hot carbonylation from cooler synthesis is sensible, but operating conditions and precursor survival during transfer remain unspecified.
suggestions: Replace the indole gap node with an experimentally supported sequence, or explicitly retain this pathway as conditional on an independently demonstrated indole source.
Test indole, pyruvate and ammonia on authentic Fe-saponite using mineral controls, isotope tracing and structural identification of tryptophan and competing products.
Specify separate carbonylation and coupling conditions and measure pyruvate delivery from the hot zone into the cooler receiving zone.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The aldehyde-to-tryptophan sequence has sound conventional Strecker logic, consistent with the general chemistry discussed by Miller (1957). Its feasibility is conditional on obtaining tryptaldehyde. Besides the unresolved indole source, rxn_008 needs demonstrated alcohol activation and cyanide capture rather than indole condensation. The decisive additional bottleneck is rxn_010: aqueous mineral/H2 chemistry has not been shown here to stop selectively at the aldehyde instead of producing tryptamine, indole acetate or other products. Imine accumulation is not essential if cyanide trapping drives the equilibrium.
suggestions: Identify a geochemically available catalyst and operating window for selective nitrile-to-aldehyde conversion, with a quantitative product balance.
Measure hydroxymethylindole formation and cyanide trapping against bis-indolylmethane formation and other condensation reactions.
Demonstrate the linked Strecker and hydrolysis steps under conditions that preserve the indole group, and quantify intermediate survival during environmental transfers.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The terminal Strecker module is credible, but the ammonia-based entry adds unresolved selectivity requirements. Familiar gramine chemistry using dimethylamine does not directly establish rxn_007 with ammonia or selective accumulation of primary 3-aminomethylindole. In rxn_009, ammonia displacement requires suitable activation and a demonstrated pH window for cyanide trapping. The unresolved indole assembly and selective nitrile reduction remain blocking dependencies. This is a plausible testing sequence, not an experimentally closed synthesis.
suggestions: Verify the identity, yield and stability of 3-aminomethylindole formed specifically from indole, formaldehyde and ammonia.
Establish cyanide-substitution kinetics and selectivity under explicitly stated activation and acid–base conditions.
Validate selective tryptaldehyde production before treating the downstream Strecker sequence as an end-to-end route from the starting feedstocks.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The substituted aminomalononitrile, aminomalonic acid and decarboxylation products have coherent carbon-skeleton relationships. Kuroda and Kobayashi (2024) supports considering this framework as a hypothesis, not as demonstrated tryptophan synthesis. HCN oligomerization does not establish an adequately concentrated or persistent aminomalononitrile pool. The major coupling uncertainty is selective C-alkylation in rxn_015 rather than N-alkylation, further oligomerization or indole condensation. Hydrolysis and decarboxylation are plausible conditional exits, but the actual substituted substrate has not been validated here.
suggestions: Quantify aminomalononitrile production, lifetime and competing oligomers under specified HCN concentrations, pH and temperature.
Establish C- versus N-alkylation selectivity and structurally identify mol_020 rather than inferring it from formula or mass alone.
Demonstrate hydrolysis/decarboxylation with indole preservation and provide an experimentally supported source of indole.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The downstream aminomalonic-acid skeleton can formally yield tryptophan, but rxn_007 and rxn_016 are unvalidated entry and coupling steps. Aminomethyl-group activation must permit ammonia departure while retaining sufficient aminomalononitrile carbon nucleophilicity; a productive operating window is not supplied. Competing N-alkylation and oligomerization also require measurement. The supplied Kuroda–Kobayashi proposal does not establish this specific ammonia-displacement sequence. Explicitly acknowledging these uncertainties is appropriate, but does not close the indole-source or coupling gaps.
suggestions: Demonstrate ammonia-based formation of mol_014 and its selective reaction with aminomalononitrile under specified conditions.
Measure the dependence of C-alkylation, N-alkylation and decomposition on pH and activation conditions.
Validate the substituted dinitrile hydrolysis and decarboxylation sequence using authentic intermediates before integrating it with precursor-generation modules.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Nitrile hydrolysis to indole acetate is chemically reasonable, but activation and reductive carboxylation remain major discontinuities. Direct reaction of a carboxylic acid with methanethiol does not establish useful thioester production in water; rxn_020 lacks specified activation chemistry or a demonstrated low-water process. In rxn_021, H2 supplies a formal reductant but not an established catalyst or mechanism for reductive carboxylation. Microbial indole-acetate conversion is biochemical precedent, not evidence for this abiotic implementation. Reductive amination of indolepyruvate is plausible by analogy, but substrate-specific selectivity remains unproven.
suggestions: Supply and experimentally validate a geochemically credible activation process for indoleacetyl methyl thioester formation.
Demonstrate mineral-mediated reductive carboxylation with labeled CO2 and identify the required catalyst, hydrogen activity and operating conditions.
Test indolepyruvate reductive amination against competing carbonyl reduction, decarboxylation and decomposition.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The molecular sequence is formally connected, but both the ammonia-based Mannich/cyanide entry and the thioester/carboxylation module require experimental validation. Indole-acetonitrile hydrolysis is the strongest central conversion; it does not establish the activation needed for rxn_020 or the low-potential catalytic chemistry needed for rxn_021. The proposed reductive-amination exit remains conditional on generating and preserving indolepyruvate. The literature supports this as a historical chemical proposal with biochemical analogies, not as a demonstrated abiotic route.
suggestions: Validate ammonia-based aminomethylation and subsequent cyanide displacement with product-specific analyses.
Specify an activation mechanism for thioester formation and a tested catalyst for reductive carboxylation.
Measure intermediate stability and delivery into the receiving reaction zones rather than assuming that nominally compatible modules can be linked.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Cody et al. (2000) and Novikov and Copley (2013) support the pyruvate/alanine module more strongly than the indole-acetate activation module. Producing alanine does not establish its productive nonenzymatic transamination with indolepyruvate. Rxn_024 is a coherent net transformation, but no effective abiotic catalyst, rate or equilibrium composition is supplied. The 'Biochemical' label does not specify a physical reaction environment, and enzymes or biological cofactors cannot be assumed. Indole assembly, thioester activation and reductive carboxylation remain upstream barriers.
suggestions: Define the transamination environment by temperature, pH, mineral composition and residence time, and demonstrate the reaction without biological catalysts.
Use labeled alanine nitrogen to distinguish true transamination from ammonia release followed by a different amination pathway.
Validate indole-acetate activation and carboxylation, and quantify preservation of pyruvate and indole-containing intermediates during transfer.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The proposed transformations connect the stated intermediates, but several essential chemical operations remain unsupported: indole assembly, ammonia-based aminomethylation, cyanide displacement, thioester activation, reductive carboxylation and nonenzymatic transamination. The supported pyruvate/alanine chemistry does not resolve those gaps. This assessment reflects the missing chemical demonstrations and operating conditions, not the number or order of reaction environments. The final transamination is not prohibited without enzymes, but its kinetics and selectivity need direct abiotic evidence.
suggestions: Validate the Mannich/cyanide, activation/carboxylation and transamination modules independently before claiming an integrated synthesis.
Specify a physically defined, anoxic transamination setting and an experimentally supported nonbiological catalyst.
Use isotope tracing and quantitative product balances to establish the intended carbon skeleton and nitrogen-transfer mechanism.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network has high structural validity: the 26 molecule nodes and 24 reaction nodes form a connected graph, IDs are used consistently, and the target is formally reachable. Accepting the supplied deterministic balance check as ground truth, all reactions conserve atoms and charge with suitable coefficients; none are conservation violations. Explicit coefficients would improve the representation. P1 provides genuine literature-supported target formation, but its empirical endpoint does not experimentally validate the other branches. The principal network-wide chemical gap is rxn_003, the unresolved indole source. Further critical uncertainties include correct-connectivity coupling in rxn_005, selective nitrile reduction in rxn_010, aminomalononitrile C-alkylation in rxn_015/rxn_016, activation and reductive carboxylation in rxn_020/rxn_021, and abiotic transamination in rxn_024. Hot/cool separation and opaque shielding are chemically sensible precautions, but the submitted network lacks quantitative reaction-specific operating conditions and demonstrated transfer, concentration and preservation efficiencies. Literature alignment is good in distinguishing observations, thermodynamic arguments and hypotheses, and in treating Bennu detection as occurrence evidence rather than a synthesis mechanism. However, reaction-level citations are largely absent, and explicit speculative labels do not substitute for experimental support. Unspecified stereochemistry is appropriate for the stated target; racemic production is not a defect. Overall, this is a useful, candid research network, but not a validated complete synthesis network. Its confidence of 0.55 is below the 0.90 network-approval threshold. P1 meets the separate 0.80 pathway threshold only.
